messages.content: I want to design a multi-tenant storage engine that isolates write latency while sharing compaction capacity and preserving crash-consistent tenant boundaries. The requirements are that each tenant’s p99 write latency stays within 2× its standalone baseline during competing compactions within quotas, and that crashes or capacity reassignment cannot cause cross-tenant data exposure or storage quota evasion.

Those are two distinct requirements for the same engine. Sharing compaction capacity must not let one tenant’s compaction activity push another tenant’s p99 write latency beyond 2× that tenant’s standalone baseline under the stated within-quota conditions. Separately, tenant ownership and storage-quota boundaries must remain intact across crashes and capacity reassignment. Meeting the latency target would not, by itself, establish that the data and quota boundaries are safe.
Can you unpack what “isolates write latency while sharing compaction capacity” means here?

The engine is multi-tenant, so tenants can contend for work associated with compaction. The goal is to share that capacity rather than assume every tenant has entirely separate compaction resources, while limiting how much the contention affects writes. The stated limit is specifically about p99 write latency during competing compactions within quotas. It does not say that compaction has no effect on writes, or that each tenant must have dedicated compaction capacity.
So isolation does not mean that a tenant’s write latency has to be identical to its standalone latency?

Right. The requirement allows degradation up to the stated comparison: the tenant’s p99 write latency should remain within 2× its standalone baseline in the specified competing-compaction condition. It is a bound on that comparison, not a promise of zero interference.
Is the baseline shared across tenants?

The wording says “its standalone baseline,” so the comparison is tenant-specific. A tenant’s p99 under competing compactions is compared with that tenant’s own standalone baseline, not with another tenant’s latency or with a single absolute latency target. No baseline measurement procedure or workload definition is specified here.
Why call out p99 rather than just saying writes should stay fast?

P99 makes the latency objective more precise: it concerns the high end of the observed write-latency distribution, rather than only an average or a general impression of responsiveness. The 2× comparison also gives the objective a specific threshold. It does not, on its own, state a separate requirement for every individual write or for other latency percentiles.
And the condition is competing compactions within quotas, not every conceivable load condition?

Yes. The stated latency target applies during competing compactions within quotas. That qualifier matters; it should not be silently broadened into a guarantee for unspecified out-of-quota behavior or every possible workload. The node does not define the quota values or the precise policy for applying them.
How should I think about sharing capacity without losing that distinction?

As a design constraint, shared compaction capacity and tenant-specific latency protection need to coexist. A design would have to account for contention arising from that shared work while respecting the within-quota condition. The goal does not prescribe a particular scheduling or resource-control mechanism, so the useful question at this level is whether any proposed approach can preserve the stated p99 bound while capacity remains shared.
Does this say we should optimize overall compaction throughput above everything else?

No. Sharing compaction capacity is part of the goal, but the node does not rank aggregate compaction throughput above the p99 write-latency requirement. Nor does it supply a throughput target. An approach that shares capacity yet misses the specified latency bound would not satisfy the latency portion merely because it performs compactions efficiently overall.
Let’s turn to the tenant boundary. What is meant by making it crash-consistent?

The tenant boundary must still have a coherent meaning after a crash. A crash must not leave data accessible to a different tenant or leave storage use in a state that lets a tenant evade its quota. The requirement concerns the state the engine can recover and enforce, not just the checks it performs while everything is running normally. It does not specify a recovery algorithm or an on-disk representation.
Is preventing data exposure the same thing as enforcing the storage quota?

They are related tenant-boundary obligations, but they are not interchangeable. Cross-tenant data exposure concerns whether one tenant can encounter another tenant’s data. Storage quota evasion concerns whether a tenant can retain or obtain storage without it being subject to its quota. The requirement explicitly calls for preventing both across crashes and capacity reassignment.
Why mention capacity reassignment separately from crashes?

Capacity reassignment changes which tenant may use some capacity. That change must not be mistaken for permission to expose data belonging to the previous tenant, and it must not create a way around storage-quota enforcement. A crash adds the possibility that such a transition is interrupted or recovered from an incomplete state. The goal covers both circumstances without specifying how reassignment is performed.
Would it be enough if ownership checks work before a crash and the system fixes accounting later?

The stated requirement does not give an exception for a period after a crash in which cross-tenant data is exposed or a tenant can evade its storage quota. Any design would need the boundary to remain enforceable through recovery, rather than rely solely on checks that were effective before the crash. That is a requirement on observable safety, not a prescribed sequence of repair steps.
Could a design meet the latency number and still fail the overall goal?

Yes. Keeping tenant p99 write latency within 2× its standalone baseline during competing compactions within quotas addresses the latency requirement. It does not establish that data remains tenant-isolated or that storage quotas remain effective across crashes and capacity reassignment. Both sides of the goal have to hold.
Conversely, could perfect tenant separation be enough if compactions make one tenant’s writes much slower?

Not if its p99 write latency exceeds the stated 2× standalone-baseline bound during competing compactions within quotas. Tenant-boundary safety cannot substitute for write-latency isolation, just as the latency bound cannot substitute for boundary safety.
What should remain explicitly unspecified at this stage?

The goal does not select a compaction scheduler, a layout, a recovery procedure, or a method for reassigning capacity. It gives no quota amounts, measured baselines, or observed latency results. Those details could matter to a future design, but none is established by this statement. What is established is the combination of shared compaction capacity, the tenant-specific p99 latency bound under the stated condition, and protection against cross-tenant exposure and storage quota evasion across crashes and capacity reassignment.
I want to be careful about the phrase “within quotas.” Does it weaken the data-exposure requirement?

No such qualification is stated for data exposure. “Within quotas” qualifies the competing-compaction condition for the p99 write-latency target. The separate safety requirement is to prevent cross-tenant data exposure and storage quota evasion across crashes and capacity reassignment. It would be a mistake to carry the latency qualifier over as permission for either safety failure.
Can you give me a concise way to check whether a proposed design is addressing the right problem, without assuming how it works?

Ask two questions. First, while tenants compete for shared compaction capacity within quotas, does each tenant’s p99 write latency stay within 2× its own standalone baseline? Second, across crashes and capacity reassignment, can the engine maintain tenant boundaries so that no tenant sees another’s data or evades its storage quota? Those questions test the stated objectives without choosing an implementation.
And if someone says that reassigned capacity is available, what boundary question should I ask?

Ask whether making that capacity available to a tenant could also make another tenant’s data visible, or allow storage use to escape quota enforcement—including if a crash occurs during the change. The requirement does not dictate how capacity becomes available; it says those outcomes must be prevented.

For that boundary question, I’m considering per-tenant WALs and encryption keys, reserved foreground I/O, fair-share compaction, and atomic manifests that bind extents to quota ownership. How do those pieces fit together as a proposal?

They address different parts of the design. Per-tenant write-ahead logs (WALs) and encryption keys separate tenants’ write histories and data access. Reserved foreground I/O is intended to protect writes from competition with background work, while fair-share compaction allows tenants to share compaction capacity. Atomic manifests would bind storage extents to quota ownership so that a crash or capacity reassignment cannot leave the engine with an ambiguous tenant boundary. This is a proposed approach, not evidence yet that either requirement is met.
Why use a separate WAL for each tenant?

A per-tenant WAL gives each tenant a distinct log for its writes rather than mixing their write records in one undifferentiated log. In this proposal, that separation supports a clearer tenant boundary during normal operation and recovery. It does not, by itself, establish a p99 latency bound or prevent every form of cross-tenant exposure; the other parts of the proposal and their behavior still matter.
And what does having per-tenant encryption keys add?

It makes access to encrypted tenant data depend on the appropriate tenant’s key. That is a separate protection from identifying which tenant owns an extent: ownership metadata says whose storage it is, while encryption keys constrain who can read its contents. The proposal includes both because neither should be treated as a substitute for the other.
Would encryption alone make capacity reassignment safe?

Not on its own. The reassigned capacity still needs an unambiguous ownership and quota status. Encryption keys address access to contents; they do not determine which tenant is charged for an extent or whether storage use is within a quota. The proposed atomic manifests are the part intended to bind extents to that ownership.
What exactly is the foreground I/O reservation supposed to protect?

It is meant to preserve I/O capacity for foreground write activity when compaction is competing for I/O. The relevant performance check remains each tenant’s p99 write latency against its own standalone baseline: during competing compactions within quotas, it must stay within 2× that baseline. The proposal does not specify the size of the reservation or claim that a particular reservation has already achieved that result.
So reserving foreground I/O and using fair-share compaction are doing different jobs?

Yes. The reservation is aimed at keeping background compaction from consuming the I/O needed by foreground work. Fair-share compaction is aimed at how tenants share the compaction capacity that remains available. They are complementary ideas: sharing background capacity need not mean letting background work take all capacity from writes, and protecting writes need not mean giving every tenant dedicated compaction capacity.
Does fair-share compaction mean every tenant gets an identical amount?

That is not specified. “Fair-share” expresses an intention to allocate shared compaction capacity fairly among tenants, but this proposal does not define a numerical split or fairness rule. It would be premature to infer equal shares, a particular scheduling algorithm, or a result for a particular workload.
Could fair-share compaction by itself guarantee the 2× p99 target?

The proposal does not establish that. Fair treatment of compaction work and protection of foreground writes are related but distinct concerns. Whether their combination keeps each tenant’s p99 write latency within 2× its standalone baseline during competing compactions within quotas remains a requirement to check, not a measured outcome stated here.
I want to understand the manifest idea more precisely. What is being bound to what?

The proposal binds extents to quota ownership in atomic manifests. In other words, the engine should not treat an extent’s presence and its tenant quota owner as unrelated facts that can become inconsistent across a crash. The word “atomic” matters because the ownership association is meant to remain coherent when state changes or is recovered. The proposal does not specify a manifest format or an update protocol.
Why say “quota ownership” instead of only “tenant ownership”?

Because the boundary has an accounting consequence as well as an access consequence. It must be clear which tenant’s quota an extent belongs to; otherwise, a tenant might retain storage without that use being counted against its quota. Binding extents to quota ownership explicitly connects the storage being used with the tenant responsible for it.
If a crash happens while capacity is being reassigned, what should the atomic-manifest proposal accomplish?

Its intended role is to avoid a recovered state in which an extent’s quota ownership is ambiguous or detached from the extent. The broader requirement is that the crash must not enable cross-tenant data exposure or storage quota evasion, including in the context of capacity reassignment. Calling for atomic manifests identifies a design direction for that boundary, without specifying exactly how an interrupted reassignment is completed or recovered.
Do the manifests also replace the need for separate encryption keys?

No. The proposed manifest association addresses ownership and quota accounting. Per-tenant encryption keys address access to encrypted data. Even a correct quota owner would not, by that fact alone, establish that another tenant cannot read the contents; conversely, encrypted contents do not, by themselves, establish correct quota ownership.
What about the WALs—do atomic manifests make those unnecessary?

The proposal includes both. Per-tenant WALs keep write logging separated by tenant, while atomic manifests bind extents to quota ownership. They concern different kinds of state. Nothing in the proposal says either one can be omitted because the other exists.
Would it be accurate to present this as the completed storage-engine design?

It would be more accurate to present it as a proposed architecture. The named components convey the intended separation of write histories and keys, protection for foreground I/O, sharing of compaction capacity, and crash-consistent extent ownership. They do not yet specify enough operational detail—or provide latency and safety results—to claim that the full engine meets its requirements.
Which parts most directly relate to the latency requirement, and which to tenant boundaries?

Reserved foreground I/O and fair-share compaction most directly address write-latency isolation while compaction capacity is shared. Per-tenant WALs, per-tenant encryption keys, and atomic manifests binding extents to quota ownership most directly address tenant separation and crash-consistent boundaries. Those groupings describe their intended roles, not a claim that the concerns are independent or that any one component proves a requirement.
If I describe the design in one sentence, can I say that the manifest is the authority for quota ownership?

You can say the proposal uses atomic manifests to bind extents to quota ownership. Calling the manifest the sole authority would add a more specific design decision than the proposal states. The important commitment here is the atomic extent-to-quota-owner association, particularly across crashes and capacity reassignment.
Then the short version is: keep tenant writes and keys separate, reserve foreground I/O, share compaction fairly, and make extent-to-quota ownership atomic?

Yes—as a description of the proposal. More precisely, it calls for per-tenant WALs and encryption keys, reserved foreground I/O, fair-share compaction, and atomic manifests binding extents to quota ownership. Those are the proposed means for pursuing the latency and boundary requirements, not a statement that the 2× p99 target or crash-safety properties have already been demonstrated.
How can compactions share I/O without pushing any in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency above 2× its standalone baseline?

The proposed approach is to protect foreground I/O while allocating compaction I/O fairly among tenants. The reservation is meant to stop shared background work from consuming the capacity writes need; fair-share compaction governs how tenants use the capacity available for compaction. But those are design ideas, not a demonstrated guarantee. The requirement is that each in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency, during competing compactions, remains within 2× that tenant’s own standalone baseline.
Does that mean compactions should only run when no writes are happening?

Not necessarily. The goal is to share compaction capacity while isolating write latency, not to prohibit compaction whenever writes occur. The reservation expresses a way to keep foreground work protected even when compaction is active. How much concurrent compaction is compatible with the latency bound is not specified here.
So the key is limiting what compaction can take from foreground writes?

That is one central idea. If background work can consume I/O needed by foreground writes without an effective limit, fair sharing among compactions alone would not protect write latency. Reserved foreground I/O addresses that distinction: compactions can share I/O, but that sharing must leave enough protection for the stated tenant-specific p99 bound.
Why isn’t a fair-share compaction policy enough by itself?

Fairness among compactions answers who gets access to shared compaction capacity. The latency question asks what happens to foreground writes while that capacity is being used. Compaction could be shared fairly among tenants and still interfere too much with their writes. The proposal therefore pairs fair-share compaction with reserved foreground I/O; neither term alone proves the 2× p99 outcome.
Should the I/O reservation be understood as a guarantee that writes always get a particular amount of capacity?

The proposal calls for reserved foreground I/O, but does not give a reservation amount or define an allocation rule. Its intended role is to protect foreground work from competing compactions. Whether a particular reservation is sufficient has to be judged against the requirement: no in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency above 2× its standalone baseline under the stated competition.
Could we just look at p99 write latency across all tenants together?

That would not directly answer the question. The bound applies to any in-quota tenant, compared with that tenant’s own standalone baseline. An aggregate p99 could obscure a tenant whose writes exceed its individual 2× bound. The comparison needs to retain the tenant boundary.
And “standalone baseline” is a comparison for each tenant, not an absolute latency ceiling?

Correct. The threshold is expressed as a ratio to each tenant’s standalone baseline. If tenants have different baselines, the requirement does not turn those into one common absolute p99 limit. It says that competing compactions within quotas must not push any tenant beyond 2× its own baseline.
What role do quotas play in the question?

They define the condition under which the stated latency bound applies: competing compactions while tenants are within quotas. The question does not supply quota amounts or specify behavior outside that condition. It would be too broad to present the 2× bound as an unconditional promise for every possible demand level.
Does being in quota automatically mean there is enough I/O to meet the bound?

The node does not establish that implication. Being within quotas identifies the tenants and condition covered by the requirement; it does not itself demonstrate that a proposed I/O allocation will keep p99 latency within 2×. The design has to reconcile the admitted competition with the required outcome rather than assuming the word “quota” makes the outcome automatic.
I’m trying to separate the sharing decision from the protection decision. Is that the right way to frame it?

Yes. One question is how compaction capacity is shared among tenants. Another is how that shared background activity is kept from imposing excessive latency on foreground writes. Fair-share compaction addresses the first; reserved foreground I/O is directed at the second. They have to work together to satisfy the specific p99 comparison.
If one tenant has more compaction work than another, does fair-share mean it may take all otherwise unused compaction I/O?

The proposal does not define that behavior. Fair-share compaction names an allocation principle, not a detailed rule for unused capacity or unequal demand. Whatever rule is chosen would still need to preserve the foreground-write protection and the bound for every covered tenant.
Could protecting foreground writes for one tenant accidentally leave another tenant above the 2× limit?

That is exactly why the wording says “any in-quota tenant.” A favorable result for one tenant, or for tenants on average, is insufficient if another covered tenant exceeds 2× its own standalone p99. The proposal has to be considered tenant by tenant during competing compactions, not only as a system-wide allocation that seems fair in aggregate.
Is the target about making compaction latency predictable too?

Not in this question. Compaction capacity is to be shared, but the numerical target concerns tenant p99 write latency. No corresponding compaction-latency threshold is stated. Fair-share compaction describes how the background capacity is intended to be shared, without adding a separate numerical performance promise for compaction.
What if foreground writes are protected most of the time but see occasional severe delays?

Those delays matter insofar as they affect p99 write latency. The requirement is not merely that writes usually feel responsive or that average latency stays low; it names p99 and a 2× comparison to each tenant’s standalone baseline. At the same time, it does not state a separate bound for every individual write.
Can reserved foreground I/O be treated as proof of the latency bound?

No. It explains the intended means of reducing interference, not the observed or guaranteed result of a fully specified design. The reservation’s details and its effectiveness are not given. The same caution applies to fair-share compaction: a sensible allocation principle is not, by itself, proof that every covered tenant stays within 2× its baseline.
Then what would a convincing answer to the question have to account for, without choosing an I/O scheduler yet?

It would have to explain how foreground writes remain protected while compactions use shared I/O, how compaction capacity is shared without overriding that protection, and why the resulting behavior satisfies the per-tenant p99 bound under competing compactions within quotas. At this point, the proposal identifies reserved foreground I/O and fair-share compaction as the relevant ideas, but it does not supply a scheduler or an established latency result.
Is it reasonable to say that sharing compaction I/O is conditional on not violating the write-latency requirement?

Yes, as a statement of the design constraint. Sharing is part of the goal, but it cannot be treated as successful if it pushes any covered tenant’s p99 write latency above 2× that tenant’s standalone baseline. That does not specify how the engine will enforce the constraint; it keeps the intended sharing subordinate to the stated latency requirement.
I don’t want to imply we’ve already found the precise split between foreground and compaction I/O.

Then keep the description at the level the proposal supports: reserve foreground I/O and share compaction capacity fairly, with the open question of how to do so while meeting the tenant-specific 2× p99 bound. No precise split, quota value, or demonstrated outcome has been specified.

Here’s a more concrete hypothesis for the compaction-I/O question: per-tenant foreground queues reserving 70% of device IOPS, together with weighted-deficit compaction, keep in-quota write p99 at or below 2× standalone. How should we state that carefully?

State it as a hypothesis, not a measured result: per-tenant foreground queues reserve 70% of device IOPS for foreground work, while weighted-deficit compaction shares background capacity; together, these are hypothesized to keep each in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency ≤2× its own standalone baseline during competing compactions. The 70% is a proposed reservation, and the latency outcome remains to be established.
Does “per-tenant foreground queues reserving 70%” mean every tenant gets 70% of the device?

No. The hypothesis describes per-tenant foreground queues and a reservation of 70% of device IOPS for foreground work. It does not say that each tenant independently receives 70% of the device, or specify how the reserved foreground IOPS are divided among those queues.
And the 70% refers specifically to device IOPS?

Yes. The stated quantity is 70% of device IOPS. It should not be restated as 70% of bandwidth, CPU time, or total system capacity. Those are different quantities, and the hypothesis does not give reservations for them.
What is the weighted-deficit part intended to do?

It is the proposed means of sharing compaction work when tenants compete for I/O. In general, weighted-deficit scheduling uses weights and tracked service to distribute opportunities over time. Here, the node names weighted-deficit compaction but does not specify the weights, accounting units, or detailed scheduling rules. Its intended role is fair sharing of compaction capacity alongside foreground protection.
So the foreground queues and weighted-deficit compaction address different kinds of contention?

They address different aspects of the same contention. The per-tenant foreground queues and 70% device-IOPS reservation are intended to protect writes from background I/O competition. Weighted-deficit compaction is intended to govern sharing among compactions. The hypothesis is that combining those aspects keeps in-quota write p99 within the 2× standalone comparison.
Can I say the other 30% is guaranteed to compactions?

Not from this wording alone. A 70% reservation for foreground IOPS identifies a protected share, but the hypothesis does not say that compactions are guaranteed exactly 30%, that they can never use otherwise idle IOPS, or how the reservation operates when demand changes. Those would be additional scheduling rules.
Does reserving 70% mean foreground writes always use all of it?

No. A reservation concerns capacity intended to be available or protected for foreground work; it is not a statement that writes continuously generate enough demand to consume 70% of device IOPS. The hypothesis does not describe what happens to unused reserved capacity.
Why keep the queues per tenant if the IOPS reservation is for foreground work overall?

Per-tenant queues keep foreground work distinguishable by tenant. That matters because the proposed outcome is also per tenant: no in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency should exceed 2× its own standalone baseline. The hypothesis does not, however, define a per-tenant share of the 70% reservation or claim that separate queues alone guarantee the outcome.
Could an aggregate write p99 make this hypothesis look successful even if one tenant has a problem?

Yes. The hypothesized bound concerns each in-quota tenant, not a pooled p99 across tenants. An aggregate can conceal a tenant whose p99 exceeds 2× its standalone baseline. The statement should retain the per-tenant comparison rather than replacing it with an overall latency figure.
Does ≤2× mean exactly twice the baseline is allowed?

Yes. The symbol ≤ includes equality: a p99 of exactly 2× that tenant’s standalone baseline is within the stated bound; a p99 above 2× is not. That comparison applies to the covered in-quota condition during competing compactions.
Is the hypothesis about average latency too?
No. Its numerical claim is about p99 write latency. It does not supply a separate average-latency target, nor does it promise that every individual write completes within twice a baseline latency.
Should I phrase this as preventing compaction interference entirely?

No. The hypothesized outcome permits some write-latency degradation, provided each in-quota tenant’s p99 stays at or below 2× its standalone baseline. The point is bounded interference while compactions share I/O, not an assertion that compaction has no effect on writes.
What does the in-quota qualifier attach to here?

It limits the write-latency claim to tenants operating within quotas under the stated competing-compaction condition. The hypothesis does not extend the ≤2× promise to unspecified out-of-quota behavior. It also does not provide the quota amounts or define a new quota policy.
Are we saying 70% is the proven minimum needed to meet the target?

No. The hypothesis proposes reserving 70% of device IOPS as part of a combination expected to meet the latency bound. It does not say that 70% has been proved sufficient, that any smaller reservation would fail, or that it is an optimal split.
Likewise, can we say weighted-deficit compaction has already been shown to work with that reservation?

No. The combination is the hypothesis. No experiment, measured p99, or demonstrated result is stated here. Naming a scheduling approach explains what might be used to share compaction I/O; it does not establish the predicted latency outcome.
Does this hypothesis also answer the crash-consistent tenant-boundary requirement?

Not by itself. This hypothesis concerns foreground queues, a 70% device-IOPS reservation, weighted-deficit compaction, and the resulting in-quota p99 write-latency bound. It does not make a claim about cross-tenant data exposure or storage quota ownership across crashes and capacity reassignment.
If I want one compact sentence that stays within the claim, what would it be?

The hypothesis is that per-tenant foreground queues reserving 70% of device IOPS, combined with weighted-deficit compaction, keep each in-quota tenant’s p99 write latency during competing compactions at or below 2× its standalone baseline.
Let’s run TenantMix-8 with a 70% foreground IOPS reservation and weighted-deficit compaction, then compare tenant write p99 against standalone under competing compactions.

That is an evaluation activity for the latency hypothesis. TenantMix-8 would run with the stated 70% foreground IOPS reservation and weighted-deficit compaction. The comparison is each tenant’s write p99 during competing compactions against that tenant’s standalone baseline. The run and its results have not been reported yet.
What question would that comparison answer?

It would show whether the observed write p99 for each covered tenant stays at or below 2× its own standalone baseline under competing compactions in TenantMix-8. That is the specific latency prediction the activity is meant to evaluate, rather than a general claim that all writes are unaffected by compaction.
Should we combine all tenant writes into one p99 for the comparison?

No. The target is tenant-specific. Pooling writes into one p99 could hide a tenant whose p99 exceeds 2× its own standalone baseline. The comparison should retain a separate write-p99 value and corresponding standalone baseline for each tenant being assessed.
Does the name TenantMix-8 tell us exactly what the workload contains?

No workload definition is given here. TenantMix-8 is the named run, but its name alone does not establish the number of tenants, their workloads, quota settings, or compaction pattern. We should not infer those details from the label.
Where do the competing compactions fit in?

They are the condition under which tenant write p99 is to be compared with standalone. The activity is not simply a latency measurement with the reservation enabled; it specifically calls for evaluating write p99 while compactions compete. It does not specify how that competition is generated.
Is the standalone value one baseline for the whole device?

The intended comparison is against each tenant’s standalone baseline, not a single device-wide number or another tenant’s result. This activity does not specify how those standalone baselines are obtained, and it provides no baseline values.
How does the 70% figure enter the run?

It is the foreground IOPS reservation specified for TenantMix-8. The quantity is 70% of device IOPS; it should not be described as 70% of bandwidth or as a guaranteed 70% allocation to every individual tenant. The activity does not define the reservation’s detailed mechanics.
And weighted-deficit compaction is active in the same run?

Yes. The activity calls for TenantMix-8 with both the 70% foreground IOPS reservation and weighted-deficit compaction. The comparison would therefore concern that stated combination, not either feature considered alone.
If a tenant’s p99 is at exactly 2× standalone, how does that relate to the hypothesis?

Exactly 2× is within the hypothesized ≤2× bound. A value above 2× would exceed it. That interpretation applies tenant by tenant under the stated competing-compaction and in-quota conditions; it is not an observed outcome of TenantMix-8 yet.
Does the run description already establish that every tenant is in quota?

No. The hypothesis concerns in-quota writes, but this activity does not report the participating tenants’ quota status. The in-quota condition matters when interpreting the comparison; the run description alone does not establish that it holds.
Could I report just that the foreground reservation was enabled and call the hypothesis confirmed?

No. Enabling the 70% reservation and weighted-deficit compaction describes the run configuration. The hypothesis concerns the resulting per-tenant write p99 relative to standalone during competing compactions. No such measurements are supplied here, so no outcome can be declared.
What should we avoid claiming before the comparison is available?

Avoid claiming that TenantMix-8 met or missed the 2× target, that 70% is sufficient or optimal, or that weighted-deficit compaction caused a particular latency result. The current node specifies an activity and a comparison, not findings.
Would the comparison tell us how well compaction itself performs?

Not as stated. The named comparison is tenant write p99 against standalone under competing compactions. It does not specify a compaction-throughput or compaction-latency result, even though weighted-deficit compaction is part of the run configuration.
Can the activity be summarized without making it sound completed?

Yes: run TenantMix-8 with a 70% foreground IOPS reservation and weighted-deficit compaction, and compare each tenant’s write p99 during competing compactions with its standalone baseline to assess the in-quota ≤2× hypothesis. That describes the planned evaluation without asserting a result.
TenantMix-8 produced an observation: in-quota tenant B’s write p99 reached 2.7× its standalone baseline during competing compactions, despite the 70% foreground IOPS reservation.

That reports a tenant-specific measurement under the stated competing-compaction condition. The 2.7× figure compares tenant B’s write p99 in TenantMix-8 with B’s own standalone baseline. The 70% foreground IOPS reservation was present, but this observation alone does not identify why B’s latency reached that value.
What does “reached 2.7× standalone” tell us in concrete terms?

It gives a ratio, not an absolute latency: tenant B’s observed write p99 reached 2.7 times its standalone write-p99 baseline. Without the baseline in time units, we cannot state the corresponding latency in milliseconds or any other absolute unit.
Does “in-quota” describe B specifically?
Yes. The reported observation identifies tenant B as in quota. It does not, by itself, report the quota status or write latency of every other tenant in TenantMix-8.
Should we say the 70% reservation was absent or misconfigured because B reached 2.7×?

No. The observation explicitly says B reached 2.7× despite a 70% foreground IOPS reservation. It gives no evidence that the reservation was absent or misconfigured, and it does not explain how the reserved IOPS were used during the run.
Can we attribute the measurement to weighted-deficit compaction?

Weighted-deficit compaction is part of the TenantMix-8 run configuration, but the reported measurement does not isolate its effect. It would be an unsupported causal claim to say that this scheduling approach, rather than another aspect of the run, produced B’s 2.7× ratio.
What role does “during competing compactions” play in the observation?

It identifies when the reported write-p99 measurement occurred. The figure is not presented as an idle-system measurement or as B’s standalone value; it is B’s result in TenantMix-8 during competing compactions, compared against its standalone baseline.
Is 2.7× a measurement for every write B issued?
No. It describes B’s p99 write latency relative to its standalone baseline. It does not say that every individual write took 2.7 times as long, or specify the latency of any particular write.
Can we generalize the 2.7× figure to all tenants in the run?
No. The evidence names in-quota tenant B. It supplies no corresponding p99 ratios for the other tenants, so B’s measurement should remain attributed to B.
Does the figure tell us whether B’s baseline changed?
